query: For structural materials intended for fusion plasma-facing components, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs high-temperature plastic strain and toughness, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations predicted relative to an unperturbed baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys for fusion plasma‐facing components, high-temperature plastic strain and toughness are primarily governed by the stability and sliding behavior of the grain boundaries. Specifically, when properly engineered by targeted thermomechanical treatments, more stable grain boundaries suppress intergranular cracking and promote controlled grain boundary sliding, thereby enabling enhanced plastic deformation and toughness. In contrast, when grain boundaries are not optimized, early intergranular failure dominates even if dislocation‐mediated plasticity is active.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a stable microstructure manufactured via a standard processing route (i.e., non-engineered grain boundaries).
generation.intervention: Apply systematic grain-boundary engineering via targeted thermomechanical treatments to modify the grain size distribution and misorientation angles while maintaining constant alloy chemistry.
generation.conditions: Testing should be done under fusion-relevant conditions: elevated temperatures (700–1200 °C) and controlled irradiation flux representative of plasma-facing components, with in situ tensile or creep experiments.
generation.structural_mediator: Engineered grain boundary stability and density (i.e., refined and controlled grain boundary misorientation distributions) that modify the onset of grain boundary sliding and intergranular cracking.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, thermal activation enhances atomic mobility particularly at grain boundaries. In the engineered alloy, optimized (stable) grain boundaries delay the onset of intergranular sliding and cavitation, which in turn improves both plastic strain and toughness. In the unperturbed baseline, disordered or weak grain boundaries lead to premature intergranular cracking despite significant dislocation activity within grains.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the unperturbed baseline, the grain boundary engineered alloys will exhibit increased plastic deformation before crack initiation, higher toughness measured by delayed intergranular crack propagation, and a shift in the failure mode from intergranular to more transgranular fracture modes under high-temperature, irradiated conditions.
generation.baseline: The baseline is the same tungsten-based refractory alloy processed via conventional thermal and mechanical treatments without targeted grain boundary control.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold for tungsten-based high-entropy alloys or similarly refractory alloys under fusion-relevant elevated temperatures (roughly 700–1200 °C) and under irradiation conditions typical of plasma-facing components. Outside this regime (e.g., at low temperatures or in non-irradiated environments), the dominant mechanisms may shift toward dislocation-mediated plasticity.
generation.uncertainty: While prior evidence indicates enhanced grain boundary slip at high temperatures, the precise quantitative contribution of engineered grain boundaries versus dislocation mechanisms remains to be precisely determined and may depend on the specifics of irradiation dose and strain rate.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy samples: one processed via conventional methods (baseline) and one with targeted thermomechanical treatments to engineer grain boundary characteristics. Subject both sets to in situ high-temperature tensile tests under irradiation conditions representative of fusion plasma-facing environments. Use high-resolution microscopy (TEM/SEM) to track microstructural evolution, focusing on grain boundary sliding, dislocation dynamics, and crack initiation sites.
measurements: Quantification of plastic strain until crack initiation
Measurement of fracture toughness and crack propagation modes
Characterization of grain boundary structure and dislocation density via TEM
In situ observation of deformation mechanisms (grain boundary sliding vs. dislocation slip)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the engineered samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature plastic strain and toughness compared to the baseline, or if intergranular failure remains the dominant mode despite improved grain boundary characteristics, then the hypothesis that grain boundary stability controls the high-temperature deformation behavior is falsified.

AbstractThe NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 is a refractory multi-principal-element alloy with high strength and good ductility at room temperature. It is important for possible high-temperature applications to investigate the deformation mechanism of the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy at different temperatures using tensile tests. In this investigation, the tensile tests were conducted at room temperature to 1273 K on sheet materials fabricated by cold rolling combined with annealing treatments. At 473 K, the NbTaHfTiZrV0.5 alloy exhibited a high tensile ductility (12%). At a testing temperature range of 673~873 K, the ductility was reduced, but the yield strength remained above 800 MPa, which is rare in most other alloys. The TEM investigations revealed that a dislocation slip controlled the plastic deformation, and the degree of deformation was closely related to the dislocation density. The true stress–strain curves of the alloy under different deformation conditions were obtained by tensile deformation at different deformation temperatures (673~873 K) and strain rates (0.001~0.0005 s−1). frame.system: Structural metallic alloys (e.g., steels, W-based alloys) for use in fusion plasma-facing components, with an initially stable microstructure and exposed to high heat and irradiation conditions.
frame.goal: Determine the governing mechanism(s) behind high-temperature plastic strain and fracture toughness, and clarify why a particular mechanism is dominant in these severe service environments.
frame.limitation: The fundamental mechanism controlling both plastic deformation and toughness under the extreme conditions of fusion reactors is not clearly established, and the relative influence of dislocation mobility, grain boundary processes, and microstructural evolution remains uncertain.

decision.trend: Recent work on tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloys for fusion plasma-facing applications has focused on advanced powder bed processes (PMC9229239::webcard, 2022) and nanoscale precipitation strategies (PMC10213035::webcard, 2023). The former demonstrated the feasibility of synthesizing WTaMoNbV alloys by combining elemental powders via laser powder bed fusion, while the latter improved both strength and high-temperature ductility through designed coherent nanoprecipitates. Despite these advances, the fundamental mechanism controlling high-temperature plastic strain and toughness remains unsettled, particularly regarding grain boundary behavior, dislocation activity, and the consequent impact on failure modes under extreme service environments.
decision.unsolved: It is still uncertain whether dislocation-driven plasticity or grain boundary processes dominate in governing elevated-temperature ductility and fracture resistance of refractory alloys in intense radiation and thermal flux. The relative contributions of grain boundary stability, dislocation nucleation/mobility, and microstructural evolution under irradiation and high temperature require further clarification.
decision.lever: Systematic grain-boundary engineering via targeted thermomechanical treatments (e.g., controlling final grain size and misorientation distributions) in a fixed W-based refractory high-entropy alloy composition, then performing high-temperature in situ mechanical tests (with and without irradiation) to compare intergranular vs. transgranular crack progression, dislocation structures, and respective contributions to plastic flow and toughness.
decision.why: Prior work has boosted high-temperature strength and ductility through processing and precipitation strategies, but the core mechanism unifying high-temperature plastic strain and toughness in tungsten-based alloys under fusion-relevant conditions remains elusive. A controlled variation of grain boundary characteristics, while keeping alloy chemistry constant, directly isolates the role of boundary processes and dislocation flow under stress and irradiation at elevated temperatures—providing a decisive test of whether grain-boundary stability and sliding behavior or purely dislocation-mediated plasticity is the governing factor.
